title: Amitriptyline and Alcohol: Risks, the 10 mg Dose, and Timing
excerpt: Can you drink on amitriptyline? How this tricyclic antidepressant and alcohol stack sedation, why the 10 mg dose still needs care, timing, and warning signs.
metaDescription: Can you drink on amitriptyline? How it and alcohol stack sedation and dizziness, whether 10 mg is okay, overdose risk, timing, and when to get help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** amitriptyline and alcohol are a risky pair, and the drug's US label warns that amitriptyline can increase your response to alcohol. Both slow down your brain, both can make you dizzy or faint when you stand up, and together they can leave you far sleepier and more unsteady than either one alone. That raises the risk of falls, accidents, and, with heavier drinking, dangerously deep sedation. Amitriptyline also belongs to an older class of antidepressants (tricyclics) that are much more dangerous than modern ones if too much is taken, and alcohol makes that danger worse. This guide explains how the two interact, why the low 10 mg dose many people take for pain or sleep still deserves care, how timing works if you've already been drinking, and which warning signs mean you should get help.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink during the first week or two on amitriptyline, or after a dose increase, until you know how it affects you. After that, whether an occasional drink is okay is a question for your prescriber, not something to work out alone. Never drink to "boost" amitriptyline if it isn't helping you sleep or easing your pain. If you've been drinking and you're due a bedtime dose, follow the plan your prescriber gave you (ask for one in advance), and never take extra to make up for a missed dose. Don't stop amitriptyline suddenly just so you can drink. If someone is very hard to wake, confused, breathing slowly, has a racing or irregular heartbeat, or has a seizure after mixing the two, call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and drug-label guidance. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who prescribed your medicine and knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking alcohol on amitriptyline,** and especially if you're older, take it at a higher dose for depression, take other sedating medicines, have a heart condition, or have had falls or fainting spells. **Call 911 or your local emergency number** if someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly, confused or agitated, has a very fast or irregular heartbeat, faints, or has a seizure. **If you think someone has taken too much amitriptyline, with or without alcohol, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US) right away, even if they seem fine.**

## What Amitriptyline Is and Why People Take It

Amitriptyline is a **tricyclic antidepressant** (often shortened to TCA). It has been around since the early 1960s, and it was once one of the main treatments for depression. Today it's prescribed in two quite different ways:

- **At higher doses for depression.** This is its original, approved use. Doses for depression are typically much higher than the doses used for pain or sleep.
- **At low doses for other conditions.** Many people take 10 mg to 25 mg (sometimes a bit more) at bedtime for nerve pain, migraine and tension headache prevention, fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, chronic pain, or trouble sleeping. Many of these uses are "off-label," meaning they aren't the official approved use, but they're common and supported by clinical experience and guidelines. In the UK, low-dose amitriptyline is a very common choice for nerve pain and headache prevention.

That split matters for this topic. Someone taking 10 mg for headaches may not think of themselves as being "on an antidepressant" at all, and may not have been told much about alcohol. But the drug is the same molecule, and it carries the same kinds of effects, just at a smaller scale.

Amitriptyline is usually taken at night because it causes drowsiness. That's often part of why it's chosen: for someone whose pain keeps them awake, a medicine that also helps them sleep can be useful. It's also the reason alcohol is a problem, since a bedtime dose and an evening of drinking tend to land in your body at the same time.

## How Amitriptyline and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Amitriptyline works on several systems in the brain and body at once. Its main antidepressant action is blocking the recycling of two chemical messengers, serotonin and norepinephrine, so more of them stay active between nerve cells. But it also blocks several other receptors, and those "side" actions are what cause most of its side effects and most of the trouble with alcohol.

### 1. Stacked sedation

Amitriptyline is a strong **antihistamine**, in the same sense that older sleep aids like diphenhydramine (Benadryl) are. Blocking histamine in the brain makes you drowsy. Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant: it boosts the brain's main calming signal (GABA) and dampens its main excitatory signal (glutamate). If you want the detail on that, our explainer on [whether alcohol is a depressant](/never-hungover/is-alcohol-a-depressant) covers it.

When you combine them, the effects add up. You may feel much sleepier, slower, and more uncoordinated than you'd expect from the amount you drank. Your judgment and reaction time drop further. At higher amounts of alcohol, or with other sedating drugs in the mix, the combination can deepen into heavy sedation where breathing slows and a person becomes hard to wake.

### 2. Dizziness and fainting when you stand up

Amitriptyline blocks receptors (called alpha-1 receptors) that help your blood vessels tighten when you stand. When those are blocked, blood pressure can drop suddenly as you get up, making you lightheaded or causing you to faint. Doctors call this **orthostatic hypotension**.

Alcohol widens blood vessels and dehydrates you, which pushes blood pressure in the same direction. Together, the classic danger moment is getting up in the night to use the bathroom: drowsy, dehydrated, and with blood pressure that drops as you stand. That's a common setup for falls and head injuries, and it's why older adults are at particular risk.

### 3. Anticholinergic effects

Amitriptyline also blocks acetylcholine, a messenger involved in memory, attention, digestion, and saliva. This is why it commonly causes dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, and trouble passing urine, and why it can cause confusion, especially in older people. Alcohol also impairs memory and attention. Stacked together, the result can be more confusion and memory gaps than you'd get from drinking alone.

### 4. Heart rhythm effects

Amitriptyline can speed up the heart and, at higher blood levels, affect the heart's electrical signals. At normal doses in a healthy person this usually isn't a serious problem, but it's the main reason tricyclics are so dangerous in overdose. Alcohol can also raise heart rate and, after heavy drinking, sometimes trigger irregular rhythms. If you notice a pounding, racing, or irregular heartbeat after drinking on amitriptyline, take it seriously. Our guide to a [racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) covers the more common, harmless causes too, but on a tricyclic the bar for getting checked should be lower.

### 5. Blood levels may change

Amitriptyline is broken down in the liver, mainly by enzymes called CYP2D6 and CYP2C19, into an active product called nortriptyline (which is itself sold as a separate antidepressant). Older pharmacology research suggests that drinking at the same time as taking amitriptyline may raise the amount of the drug in your bloodstream for a while, which would add to sedation and impairment. The size of this effect varies from person to person, and it's not something you can predict or adjust for on your own. The practical lesson is simple: the combination can hit harder than you expect.

## What the Label and Official Guidance Actually Say

The US prescribing information for amitriptyline warns that it may enhance the response to alcohol and to other drugs that slow down the nervous system, such as barbiturates. It also warns that amitriptyline can impair the mental and physical abilities needed for driving or operating machinery.

UK NHS patient guidance takes a similar line. It explains that alcohol can make you feel sleepier on amitriptyline, and it suggests not drinking during the first few days of treatment until you see how the medicine affects you.

So the official message isn't always "never a single drop," but it's clearly "be careful, and expect a stronger effect." Your prescriber may give stricter advice depending on your dose, your age, why you take it, and what else you take.

Like all antidepressants, amitriptyline's US label also carries a boxed warning about a possible increase in suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, teens, and young adults, especially when starting or changing the dose. Alcohol can lower inhibition and worsen low mood, which is one more reason to be cautious during those early weeks.

## Can You Drink on Amitriptyline 10 mg?

This is one of the most searched questions, because so many people take the low dose for pain, migraines, or sleep and want to know if an occasional drink is okay.

The honest answer: **the risk at 10 mg is lower than at depression doses, but it isn't zero, and it's a question for your prescriber.** Here's what shifts the picture:

- **The sedating effects show up even at low doses.** Many people notice grogginess, a "drugged" feeling, or dry mouth on 10 mg, especially in the first couple of weeks. Alcohol adds to exactly those effects.
- **Timing usually overlaps.** A bedtime dose taken after an evening of drinking means both are peaking in your body at the same time.
- **Your own sensitivity matters.** Some people break amitriptyline down slowly because of their genes (they have less active CYP2D6 or CYP2C19 enzymes), so even a low dose leaves more of the drug in their system. You usually can't know this without testing.
- **Dose increases change things.** Low doses for pain are often raised gradually, to 20, 25, 50 mg, or more. Each step up brings more sedation, so what felt fine at 10 mg may not at a higher dose.

Some prescribers are comfortable with an occasional light drink for people on a stable low dose who know how the medicine affects them. Others will advise against alcohol altogether. Neither answer is wrong; it depends on you.

### If your prescriber says an occasional drink is okay

These steps lower (but don't remove) the risk:

1. **Wait until you're settled on the dose.** Don't drink during the first week or two, or after any dose increase.
2. **Stick to the amount your prescriber agreed,** and treat it as a limit, not a starting point. A standard drink is roughly 12 oz of regular beer, 5 oz of wine, or 1.5 oz of spirits.
3. **Drink early in the evening and with food,** so there's more time between the drink and your bedtime dose.
4. **Expect it to feel stronger than usual.** Don't drive, bike, or do anything risky afterwards, even if you feel okay.
5. **Get up slowly,** especially at night. Sit on the edge of the bed for a moment before standing.
6. **Don't combine it with other sedating things,** like sleep aids, allergy pills that cause drowsiness, cannabis, or anxiety medicines.

## Amitriptyline at Depression Doses and Alcohol

At the higher doses used for depression, the case against drinking is stronger, for three reasons:

- **The effects are bigger.** More drug means more sedation, more blood-pressure drop, and more anticholinergic and heart effects for alcohol to add to.
- **Alcohol works against the treatment.** Alcohol tends to worsen depression and anxiety over time, even if a drink seems to help in the moment. It also fragments sleep in the second half of the night, which matters when sleep is part of what's being treated. Our overview of [antidepressants and alcohol](/never-hungover/antidepressants-and-alcohol) covers this pattern across different medicines.
- **Overdose risk is a real concern.** Tricyclics are much more dangerous in overdose than newer antidepressants like SSRIs, and alcohol lowers inhibition and deepens sedation. That's a combination clinicians take seriously, especially for anyone going through a hard time.

If you're taking amitriptyline for depression, ask your prescriber directly whether any alcohol is okay for you. Many will advise avoiding it, at least until your mood is stable.

## Overdose: Why Tricyclics Deserve Extra Respect

This is the part of the topic people rarely hear about, and it's the main reason amitriptyline is treated differently from many other medicines.

Tricyclic antidepressants have a **narrow safety margin**. The gap between a helpful dose and a dangerous one is smaller than with most modern antidepressants. In overdose, amitriptyline can cause seizures, very low blood pressure, coma, and life-threatening heart rhythm problems. Alcohol taken at the same time adds to the sedation and can make the overall picture more dangerous. Because of this risk, doctors are often careful about how many tablets they prescribe at once to people who may be at risk.

None of this means that someone taking their normal dose and having a drink is in danger of an overdose. It means:

- **Never take extra amitriptyline** to make up for a missed dose or to help you sleep after drinking.
- **Keep it away from children.** Even a small number of tablets can be very dangerous for a child.
- **Store it safely** if anyone in the home is struggling with their mental health.
- **If someone may have taken too much,** with or without alcohol, call 911 or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) right away, even if they look fine. Symptoms can come on quickly and get worse fast.

If you're having thoughts of harming yourself, you can call or text **988** (the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the US) at any time, or contact your local emergency number.

## I Already Drank. Should I Take My Amitriptyline Tonight?

This is the most practical question, and the best time to answer it is before it comes up. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist for a plan for nights when you've been drinking.

Without that plan, here's general guidance many pharmacists would give, though it isn't a substitute for your own prescriber's advice:

- **If you take a low dose for pain, migraine, or sleep,** ask your prescriber ahead of time what to do with your bedtime dose on a night you've been drinking. Some prescribers advise leaving out that night's low dose; that's their call to make for you, not a rule to apply on your own. Never take a double dose the next night.
- **If you take a higher dose for depression,** ask your prescriber ahead of time. Missing doses repeatedly isn't a good way to treat depression, and suddenly stopping can cause unpleasant discontinuation symptoms.
- **If you've had only one drink with dinner** and your prescriber has said that's okay, taking your usual dose at your usual time may be fine. Still expect to feel drowsier than normal.
- **Never take extra** to "knock yourself out" after drinking. That's how a manageable situation becomes a dangerous one.

If you're unsure on the night, most community pharmacies can give quick advice by phone, and in the US, Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) answers questions about medication combinations, not just poisonings.

## How Long After Drinking Can You Take Amitriptyline?

There's no official waiting period that applies to everyone. Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies widely with body size, food, sex, liver health, and how fast you drank. After several drinks, alcohol can still be in your system well into the night.

The goal is to avoid having both active at once. If you've had a single drink early in the evening, by your usual bedtime most of it may be gone. If you've had several drinks, especially later in the night, the safer plan is usually not to take the dose that night (see the section above), rather than trying to calculate a gap.

## How Long After Taking Amitriptyline Can You Drink?

Amitriptyline lasts a long time in the body. Its half-life (the time it takes for the amount in your blood to fall by half) is commonly reported at roughly 10 to 28 hours in adults, and its active breakdown product, nortriptyline, lasts even longer. It can be longer still in older adults and people who process it slowly.

That means:

- **There's no "safe window" in a normal day.** If you take amitriptyline every night, there's always some in your system. A drink at 6 p.m. isn't separate from last night's dose; it's on top of it.
- **The real question is whether drinking is okay for you at all** while you're on it. That's one for your prescriber.
- **After stopping amitriptyline,** it can take several days for it to clear completely. If you've stopped (with your doctor's guidance), it's sensible to wait a few days before drinking at your old level, and to expect lower tolerance at first.

## Amitriptyline, Alcohol, and the Next Morning

Amitriptyline is known for causing a "hangover" feeling of its own: grogginess, heavy limbs, and a slow start the morning after a dose, especially early in treatment. Add actual alcohol and the next morning can feel much worse than usual.

Here's why the two pile up:

- **Grogginess on grogginess.** Lingering drug sedation plus alcohol's disrupted sleep makes for a foggy, slow morning.
- **Dry mouth and dehydration.** Amitriptyline dries your mouth; alcohol makes you lose fluid. Together you may wake up very thirsty with a headache.
- **Dizziness on standing.** Dehydration makes the blood-pressure drop from amitriptyline worse, so standing up quickly can make you lightheaded.
- **Constipation.** Amitriptyline slows the gut, and dehydration makes that worse.
- **A faster heartbeat.** Both can raise heart rate, which some people notice as a pounding pulse the next morning.

What helps: drink water steadily, eat something simple, get up slowly, and give it time. **Don't drive until you feel fully alert,** and remember that you may still be impaired even if you feel okay. Be careful with over-the-counter hangover remedies too. Some sleep aids and allergy medicines contain diphenhydramine or doxylamine, which add to amitriptyline's sedating and anticholinergic effects. Plain pain relievers have their own cautions after drinking, which our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains.

## Can Amitriptyline Help With Sleep After Drinking?

Some people who already have amitriptyline at home are tempted to take it (or an extra dose) to get to sleep after a night out, when alcohol has them wired or waking at 3 a.m. Please don't. Alcohol is still in your system at that point, so you'd be stacking sedation, and extra doses of a tricyclic carry real overdose risk.

Alcohol-related insomnia usually comes from your brain rebounding as the alcohol wears off, along with dehydration and a full bladder. It typically passes by the next night. Our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) covers safer ways to handle it. If you regularly need something to sleep, talk to your doctor about a plan that doesn't involve alcohol.

## Other Medicines That Make the Combination Riskier

The risk rises sharply when amitriptyline and alcohol are combined with other drugs that slow the brain, affect serotonin, or change how amitriptyline is broken down. Tell your prescriber and pharmacist about everything you take, including over-the-counter products and supplements. Watch for these in particular:

- **Opioid pain medicines** (such as oxycodone, hydrocodone, codeine, or tramadol). These deepen sedation and slow breathing. Tramadol also affects serotonin and can lower the seizure threshold, which adds to amitriptyline's own risks.
- **Gabapentin and pregabalin.** These are often prescribed alongside amitriptyline for nerve pain, and both add sedation and dizziness. Our page on [gabapentin and alcohol](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol) covers that interaction on its own.
- **Benzodiazepines and sleep medicines** (such as alprazolam, lorazepam, diazepam, or zolpidem). See our guide to [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol) for why those combinations are especially risky.
- **Sedating antihistamines and sleep aids** containing diphenhydramine or doxylamine. These add sedation and more anticholinergic side effects, which can cause confusion, especially in older adults.
- **Other antidepressants.** Some, such as fluoxetine, paroxetine, and bupropion, slow the liver enzyme that breaks down amitriptyline, which can raise its levels. Combining it with other serotonin-boosting drugs also raises the risk of serotonin syndrome. MAO inhibitors should not be combined with amitriptyline.
- **Medicines that affect heart rhythm.** Some antibiotics, antipsychotics, and heart medicines can affect the heart's electrical signals, as can amitriptyline. Your pharmacist can check for these.
- **Cannabis.** It can add drowsiness, dizziness, and a faster heart rate.

If you're on any of these and you also drink, that's a conversation to have with your prescriber before your next drink, not after.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

Some people face higher risk from amitriptyline and alcohol together:

- **Adults over 65.** Older adults are more sensitive to sedation, confusion, and blood-pressure drops, and falls can cause serious injuries. The American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria lists amitriptyline among medicines that are often best avoided in older adults because of its anticholinergic and sedating effects.
- **People with heart conditions,** including heart rhythm problems or a recent heart attack.
- **People with epilepsy or a history of seizures,** since tricyclics can lower the seizure threshold and heavy drinking or alcohol withdrawal can also trigger seizures.
- **People taking amitriptyline for depression,** especially if they're going through a hard time.
- **People with liver problems,** who may clear both amitriptyline and alcohol more slowly.
- **People with glaucoma (the narrow-angle type) or trouble passing urine,** which anticholinergic effects can worsen.
- **Anyone who drives, operates machinery, or cares for others** soon after taking a dose.
- **Anyone who regularly drinks heavily.** If you drink most days and find it hard to cut back, tell your doctor. That's useful medical information, and they can help you plan safely.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help

Most people who have a drink on a low dose of amitriptyline will simply feel sleepier and more unsteady than usual. But know the signs that something more serious is happening.

**Call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away if someone:**

- Is very hard to wake or can't be woken
- Is breathing slowly, shallowly, or irregularly
- Has a very fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat, or chest pain
- Faints or collapses
- Has a seizure
- Is severely confused, agitated, or seeing things that aren't there
- Has very large pupils, hot and dry skin, and a racing heart (signs that can point to tricyclic toxicity)
- May have taken more amitriptyline than prescribed, especially with alcohol

If you're with someone who's very drowsy after mixing the two, don't leave them alone to "sleep it off." Lay them on their side in the recovery position, check their breathing, and call for help if you're worried.

**Talk to your doctor or pharmacist soon if you notice:**

- Feeling much more drowsy, dizzy, or confused than usual after drinking
- Lightheadedness or near-fainting when you stand up
- Falls, even if you weren't hurt
- Worsening mood, anxiety, or new thoughts of self-harm (if you have thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US right away)
- Signs of serotonin syndrome if you take other serotonin-affecting drugs: agitation, shivering, sweating, muscle twitching, diarrhea, or fever

## Don't Stop Amitriptyline Just to Drink

If you've got a wedding, holiday, or big night coming up, it can be tempting to skip a few days of amitriptyline so you can drink "normally." That's usually a bad trade. Stopping suddenly, particularly at higher doses or after long-term use, can cause discontinuation symptoms such as nausea, headache, feeling generally unwell, and disturbed sleep. It can also bring back the pain, headaches, or low mood the medicine was controlling. And because amitriptyline lasts a long time in the body, a few skipped days won't fully clear it anyway.

If alcohol is important to you for a specific event, raise it with your prescriber ahead of time. They can tell you what's realistic for your situation.

## Living Well on Amitriptyline Without Leaning on Alcohol

If you take amitriptyline for pain, migraines, or sleep, alcohol can quietly work against your treatment. For some people, alcohol (red wine especially) is a migraine trigger. It disrupts sleep in the second half of the night, which can make pain feel worse the next day. And it can worsen mood over time.

If you want to keep socializing, alcohol-free beers, wines, and spirits have come a long way, and a lot of people find that the drink in their hand matters more than what's in it. If you do drink with your prescriber's okay, keep it light and early in the evening, eat first, alternate with water, and give yourself a clear plan for your dose that night.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Some readers who drink socially ask about DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's sold as a hangover supplement. Here's the honest picture:

- Research on DHM comes mostly from animal and lab studies, including work suggesting it affects how the brain responds to alcohol and supports alcohol metabolism. Human evidence is limited.
- **There is no good evidence that DHM makes it safe to combine amitriptyline and alcohol.** It doesn't cancel out sedation, it doesn't protect your blood pressure or heart rhythm, and it's not a reason to drink on amitriptyline.
- DHM has its own possible effects on brain GABA signaling, and it hasn't been studied alongside amitriptyline. **If you take amitriptyline or any other prescription medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist before adding DHM.** Our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known.

If you're on no sedating medicines and you're simply looking for something to support a night out, our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically use it, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. A widely used option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20); a higher-priced combination formula is [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20). Neither replaces the basics in our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover): drinking less, drinking slower, eating, and staying hydrated.

## The Bottom Line

- Amitriptyline and alcohol both cause sedation and can drop your blood pressure when you stand. Together they increase drowsiness, dizziness, confusion, falls, and, at higher amounts, the risk of dangerous oversedation.
- The US label warns that amitriptyline can enhance the response to alcohol. UK NHS guidance suggests not drinking in the first few days. Whether an occasional light drink is okay for you is a question for your prescriber.
- The low 10 mg dose used for pain, migraine, and sleep carries less risk than depression doses, but it still adds to alcohol's effects, especially because it's usually taken at bedtime.
- Tricyclics are dangerous in overdose. Never take extra amitriptyline after drinking, and call 911 or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) if someone may have taken too much.
- Adding other sedatives (opioids, gabapentin, benzodiazepines, sleep aids, sedating antihistamines) makes the combination much riskier.
- Call 911 for anyone who is hard to wake, breathing slowly, has a racing or irregular heartbeat, faints, or has a seizure after mixing the two.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking amitriptyline?**

It's best to be cautious. The US label warns that amitriptyline can increase your response to alcohol, and UK NHS guidance suggests not drinking in the first few days of treatment. Both cause drowsiness and dizziness, so together they raise the risk of falls and accidents. Some prescribers allow an occasional light drink for people settled on a low dose, so ask yours what's appropriate for you.

**Is it okay to drink on amitriptyline 10 mg?**

The risk at 10 mg is lower than at depression doses, but it's not zero. Even low doses cause drowsiness, and a bedtime dose usually overlaps with evening drinking. If your prescriber says an occasional drink is okay, stick to the amount they agreed, drink early with food, expect a stronger effect, and don't drive afterwards.

**What happens if you take amitriptyline after drinking?**

Most often, people feel much sleepier, more unsteady, and more confused than usual, get dizzy when they stand up, and wake up very groggy. Falls are a real risk, especially at night. With heavier drinking or other sedatives, the risk of dangerous oversedation and heart rhythm problems rises. Call 911 if someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly, has a racing or irregular heartbeat, or has a seizure.

**Should I skip my amitriptyline dose if I've been drinking?**

Ask your prescriber ahead of time what to do with your dose on a night you've been drinking; for low doses some prescribers advise leaving out that night's dose, but that's their decision to make for you, and you shouldn't double up the next night. If you take a higher dose for depression, ask your prescriber ahead of time what to do, since missing doses repeatedly isn't a good plan. Never take extra after drinking.

**How long after taking amitriptyline can I drink alcohol?**

Amitriptyline's half-life is commonly reported at roughly 10 to 28 hours, and its active breakdown product lasts longer. If you take it every night, there's always some in your system, so there's no truly separate window. The real question is whether drinking is okay for you at all while on it, which is one for your prescriber.

**Can amitriptyline and alcohol kill you?**

It's possible, mainly in overdose. Tricyclic antidepressants like amitriptyline are much more dangerous in overdose than newer antidepressants, and alcohol adds to the sedation. Taking a normal dose and having a drink is very unlikely to be fatal, but it does raise the risk of falls and accidents. If anyone may have taken too much amitriptyline, call 911 or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) right away.

**Why do I feel so hungover on amitriptyline after just a couple of drinks?**

Amitriptyline often causes next-morning grogginess and dry mouth on its own, and it can make you dizzy when you stand. Alcohol adds dehydration, broken sleep, and headache, and drinking alongside amitriptyline may also raise its blood levels for a while. Drink water, eat something, get up slowly, and don't drive until you feel fully alert.

**Does DHM make it safe to drink on amitriptyline?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM reduces the sedation, blood-pressure, or heart effects of combining amitriptyline and alcohol, and DHM hasn't been studied alongside amitriptyline. If you take amitriptyline or any prescription medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist before adding DHM or any other supplement.

faq.question: Should I skip my amitriptyline dose if I've been drinking?
faq.answer: Ask your prescriber ahead of time what to do with your dose on a night you've been drinking; for low doses some prescribers advise leaving out that night's dose, but that's their decision to make for you, and you shouldn't double up the next night. If you take a higher dose for depression, ask your prescriber ahead of time what to do, since missing doses repeatedly isn't a good plan. Never take extra after drinking.

faq.question: How long after taking amitriptyline can I drink alcohol?
faq.answer: Amitriptyline's half-life is commonly reported at roughly 10 to 28 hours, and its active breakdown product lasts longer. If you take it every night, there's always some in your system, so there's no truly separate window. The real question is whether drinking is okay for you at all while on it, which is one for your prescriber.

faq.question: Can amitriptyline and alcohol kill you?
faq.answer: It's possible, mainly in overdose. Tricyclic antidepressants like amitriptyline are much more dangerous in overdose than newer antidepressants, and alcohol adds to the sedation. Taking a normal dose and having a drink is very unlikely to be fatal, but it does raise the risk of falls and accidents. If anyone may have taken too much amitriptyline, call 911 or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) right away.

faq.question: Why do I feel so hungover on amitriptyline after just a couple of drinks?
faq.answer: Amitriptyline often causes next-morning grogginess and dry mouth on its own, and it can make you dizzy when you stand. Alcohol adds dehydration, broken sleep, and headache, and drinking alongside amitriptyline may also raise its blood levels for a while. Drink water, eat something, get up slowly, and don't drive until you feel fully alert.

faq.question: Does DHM make it safe to drink on amitriptyline?
faq.answer: No. There is no good evidence that DHM reduces the sedation, blood-pressure, or heart effects of combining amitriptyline and alcohol, and DHM hasn't been studied alongside amitriptyline. If you take amitriptyline or any prescription medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist before adding DHM or any other supplement.
